reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: Caused by ingestion of aristolochic acid, a nephrotoxin and carcinogen found in Aristolochia-containing herbal remedies and slimming preparations
Originally described as 'Chinese herb nephropathy' and now understood to share its mechanism with Balkan endemic nephropathy
Produces a rapidly or subacutely progressive hypocellular interstitial fibrosis with tubular atrophy, often out of proportion to glomerular changes
Presents with progressive renal impairment, mild tubular proteinuria, glycosuria and relatively bland urinary sediment
Strongly associated with upper-tract urothelial carcinoma, frequently multifocal, mediated by aristolochic-acid-DNA adducts and a characteristic mutational signature
A careful exposure history to herbal, traditional or weight-loss products is essential, as patients may not regard these as drugs
There is no specific antidote, so care rests on immediate cessation of exposure, supportive treatment and long-term urothelial cancer surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Aristolochic acid is absorbed after ingestion and metabolised to reactive nitrenium intermediates that bind covalently to DNA, forming stable aristolactam-DNA adducts. In the kidney these adducts and reactive metabolites injure proximal tubular epithelial cells, provoking apoptosis and a fibrogenic response that produces extensive, characteristically paucicellular interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy with comparatively preserved glomeruli. The same DNA adducts persist in urothelial cells and generate a distinctive A-to-T transversion mutational signature, including in TP53, driving multifocal upper-tract urothelial carcinoma. Because the adducts are long-lived, renal fibrosis and cancer risk can progress even after exposure stops.
additionalDifferentials: Balkan endemic nephropathy (same toxin, endemic setting)
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history of herbal, traditional and weight-loss product use
Renal function and quantification of tubular proteinuria, with urine glucose
Renal ultrasound assessing kidney size and cortical thinning
Urine cytology and upper-tract imaging for urothelial carcinoma surveillance
Renal biopsy showing hypocellular interstitial fibrosis with tubular atrophy
Aristolactam-DNA adduct detection or mutational signature analysis where available
redFlags: Haematuria or an upper-tract filling defect suggesting urothelial carcinoma
Rapidly progressive renal failure after recent herbal ingestion
Continued or recurrent exposure to the offending product
reference.prognosis: Renal impairment is often progressive and may advance to end-stage kidney disease despite stopping the toxin, reflecting the persistence of DNA adducts and established fibrosis. The major long-term hazard is multifocal upper-tract urothelial carcinoma, which necessitates lifelong surveillance and dominates the overall prognosis.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about herbal or traditional remedies that patients do not consider medications
Overlooking upper-tract urothelial carcinoma by omitting cytology and imaging follow-up
Assuming cessation of exposure prevents further renal or urothelial injury
Missing tubular proteinuria and glycosuria because albuminuria is modest
Not recognising the shared mechanism with Balkan endemic nephropathy
